title: Buy Clothes Online in Pakistan Without the 'What If It Doesn't Fit' Anxiety
author: Omar Farooq
authorBio: Founder of BazaarNow. Runs a store with 798 fashion items. Still buys his own shalwar kameez from a physical shop because 'the fabric feels different in person.' Knows this makes him a hypocrite. Has made peace with it.
excerpt: 798 fashion items, zero fitting room anxiety. How to buy clothes online in Pakistan without getting the wrong size, the wrong fabric, or the wrong shade of beige that was definitely 'cream' in the photo.

sections.content: Buying clothes online in Pakistan used to be a two-word conversation: 'size kya?' Followed by the seller's inevitable reply: 'fit hojayega.' It never fit. The shirt was either two sizes too small or large enough to double as a family tent. The fabric that looked like lawn in the photo turned out to be something invented in a laboratory that doesn't breathe and makes a crinkly sound when you move. This post is about never having that experience again. 798 fashion products later, here's what we know about buying clothes online in Pakistan — what works, what doesn't, and why the fitting room is now in your living room.

sections.title: The Short Version
items: Check the size chart — not the size label. Pakistani 'Large' from one brand is another brand's 'Medium.' The chart is the truth. The label is a suggestion
Fabric descriptions tell you more than photos. Look for '100% cotton,' 'linen blend,' 'fleece' — and avoid anything that just says 'premium quality fabric' without specifying what it actually is
COD means you inspect before you pay. Open the package. Touch the fabric. Hold it up. Then pay. That's not being difficult — that's the whole point of COD
BazaarNow has 798 fashion products with a 7-day return policy. If it doesn't fit, send it back. No 'but sir, size to theek hai' argument. Just a return

sections.text: The size problem is real — and it's not your body's fault

sections.content: Pakistani clothing sizes are a work of fiction. One brand's Medium is another brand's Extra Large. One brand's '32-inch waist' is 30 inches. Another's is 35. There is no national standard. There is no regulatory body. There is only chaos, tape measures, and the quiet desperation of a man holding up a kameez that's supposed to be his size but reaches his knees when it should reach his hips. (Speaking from experience. The kameez is still in my wardrobe. It mocks me.)

The solution: ignore the size label entirely. Look at the measurements. Every product at BazaarNow lists actual measurements where available — chest width in inches, length in inches, sleeve length. Not 'fits 38-42 chest.' That range means it'll fit someone with a 38 chest and also someone with a 42 chest, which is mathematically impossible unless the fabric stretches like a rubber band. Which it doesn't. Because it's cotton. Cotton doesn't stretch. Cotton tells the truth. The measurement chart is the truth. Trust the chart. The chart is your friend. The chart won't ghost you after you send the money.

sections.text: Fabric photos lie. Fabric descriptions sometimes tell the truth

sections.content: A product photo can make polyester look like silk. Studio lighting. Professional models. Photoshop. The fabric could be a dishcloth and you wouldn't know until it arrives. This is why you read the description, not just look at the photos.

Genuine fabric descriptions use specific words: '100% cotton,' 'silk blend (70% silk, 30% viscose),' 'fleece-lined,' 'leather upper.' These are verifiable. If you receive the product and the fabric doesn't match the description, you have grounds for a return. Fabric descriptions that mean nothing: 'premium quality,' 'soft touch,' 'comfortable feel,' 'export quality.' These are adjectives. Adjectives are not materials. You can't return a shirt because it wasn't 'premium' enough. You can return a shirt because it was described as 100% cotton and it's actually 100% plastic.

sections.text: Which clothes are safe to buy online — and which aren't

items: T-shirts, sweatshirts, hoodies — cotton blends, forgiving sizes. If it's slightly loose, it's 'oversized fit.' If it's slightly tight, it's 'slim fit.' Either way, it works
Tracksuits — elastic waistbands forgive all measurement errors. The most online-shopping-friendly garment ever invented

Jackets and coats — designed to be worn over other clothes. Some extra room is expected. Some extra room is actually the style. Designer intention, not sizing error. (This is my story and I'm sticking to it)
Accessories — handbags, wallets, watches. No sizing issues. No fitting anxiety. The safest online purchase in fashion
Shoes — but only if you know your exact size in that brand. Shoe sizes are surprisingly consistent within brands. Between brands, they're a lottery. Know your brand before buying online

sections.text: Think twice before buying these online:

items: Formal shalwar kameez — the fit is very specific. Shoulder width, sleeve length, kameez length, shalwar drape. Four variables. Each one can go wrong. Buy from a store where you can try it on, or a brand you've worn before

Bridal wear and formal lehengas — the most expensive clothing purchase most Pakistanis make. The fitting sessions are part of the process. Don't skip them. This is not the purchase to optimize for convenience
Anything labelled 'free size' — which usually means 'one size fits some.' You're gambling. Sometimes you win. Sometimes you give the item to your younger cousin. The younger cousin always wins

sections.text: Eid, weddings, and the seasonal shopping panic

sections.content: Two weeks before Eid, Pakistan's online clothing market becomes a pressure cooker. Everyone needs three outfits. Everyone needs them delivered yesterday. Prices spike. Scammers emerge from hibernation. The 'Eid special collection' that looked amazing on Instagram arrives three days after Eid — when you no longer need it and the seller has already changed their WhatsApp DP to a picture of a cloud.

Shop for Eid and wedding season at least 3-4 weeks in advance. The delivery takes 2-4 working days normally, but during peak season, add a buffer. The courier companies are overwhelmed. Every order in the country is moving on the same three days. Your package is in a van somewhere between Lahore and Karachi, sharing space with 47 other Eid outfits and someone's blender. Be the person who planned ahead. Be the person who is calm on Chaand Raat while everyone else is refreshing their tracking page. This is aspirational. Aim for it.

You need an exact, tailored fit — and you're not willing to use the return policy if it doesn't work. Online clothing shopping is for people who understand that returns exist for a reason. Order. Try on. Keep or return. That's the cycle. If the thought of returning something feels like a personal failure, online clothes shopping isn't for you. (And that's fine. Physical stores exist. They have fitting rooms. They have uncles sitting outside the trial room scrolling Facebook. It's an experience. Enjoy it.)

Also: don't buy clothes online if you need them for an event that starts in 3 hours. Go to the physical bazaar. Touch the fabric. Negotiate with the shopkeeper. Drink the complimentary chai. Online shopping rewards planning, not panic. We'll be here when you're shopping for the next event — the one that's three weeks away and you're being admirably proactive about. (That's the energy. Channel it.)

sections.content: Clothes are the product category where COD matters most. You need to touch the fabric. Hold it up to the light. Check the stitching. Hold it against yourself and squint at your reflection in the window. (Everyone does this. The rider has seen worse. The rider has seen someone try on a full shalwar kameez in their driveway. Your modest window-reflection squint is not even memorable.)

items.q: How do I know my size when buying clothes online?
items.a: Measure yourself with a tape measure — chest, waist, hips, sleeve length. Compare against the size chart on the product page. Ignore the S/M/L/XL label. Go by the inches. If you're between sizes, size up. Looser is fixable. Tighter is not.

items.q: What if the color looks different from the photo?
items.a: Screens display colors differently. Phone screens, laptop screens, and reality all disagree on what 'navy blue' looks like. If the color difference is significant, you can return it under our standard policy. We recommend checking the product photos on a laptop if color accuracy matters a lot — phone screens tend to oversaturate.

items.a: No. We sell ready-made products. We don't offer custom stitching. If you need tailored clothing — a fitted suit, a bridal lengha, a custom shalwar kameez — go to a physical tailor. Some things are better done in person, with pins, and three fitting sessions. We're not that store. We're the store for everything else.
